standard_prerequisites.name: Comparison of measures
standard_prerequisites.statement: If one measure is dominated by another then the integral of an increasing function against the first is at most its integral against the second.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the step that converts the domination nu <= mu into the inequality at source line 1916.

standard_prerequisites.name: Distribution functions
standard_prerequisites.statement: The mass identity and the domination are checked on the cumulative distribution functions of mu and nu.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are computed explicitly at source line 1916.

standard_prerequisites.name: Indicator functions of intervals
standard_prerequisites.statement: Positive combinations and limits of indicator functions of intervals generate the positive measurable functions used here.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the test functions in the equality analysis at source line 1918.

core_obligations: Introduce the measures mu := f la and nu := (1/(b-a)) times the integral of f la, which have the same mass (source line 1916).
Show nu <= mu by computing the cumulative distribution functions for c in the interval, using that f is increasing (source line 1916).
Since g is increasing, deduce the integral inequality from the domination (source line 1916).

For the equality statement, note that equality holds when f or g is constant, and that if f is not constant then the equality in the intermediate step holds for the indicators of intervals beginning at c if and only if c is an endpoint; conclude for positive combinations and then for limits (line 1918).

proof_roadmap.step: Build the comparison measures and verify domination through distribution functions.
Analyse equality through indicator functions, combinations and limits.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is Lemma 4.17 at source lines 1905-1912: for a < b and positive bounded increasing functions f, g on the interval, the mean of f g is at least the product of the means, with equality if and only if f or g is constant. The author's proof (source lines 1914-1920) has two parts of different character: the inequality is obtained by constructing two measures of equal mass and showing that one dominates the other through an explicit computation of their cumulative distribution functions, which uses monotonicity of f (line 1916), and then integrating the increasing function g against the dominating measure; the equality analysis is a separate argument that reduces to indicators of intervals [c,b], shows that equality forces c to be an endpoint unless f is constant, and extends the conclusion to positive combinations and then to limits (line 1918). The statement records the inequality and the equality case but neither the comparison of measures nor the reduction to indicators.
